section_summary.extract_value: This section discusses the findings of a single study that examined the psychometric properties of a Polish translation of the BAS-2. The study supported a one-dimensional factor structure and scalar invariance across sex, found adequate internal consistency, and convergent validity with other measures. Limitations included accidental sampling and self-reported BMI, with suggestions for future research on measurement invariance and behavioral indicators.
section_summary.evidence_source: 4. Discussion This study examined the factor structure and psychometric properties of a Polish translation of the BAS-2. EFA and CFA supported a one-dimensional factor structure of the BAS-2, which is in line with the original, English version of the scale (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015). Furthermore, the analyses revealed full scalar invariance across sex. Men and women did not differ significantly in total scores, as found with Spanish (Swami et al., 2017) and Chinese adults (Swami et al., 2016). This result is inconsistent with most reports that demonstrate higher scores in men with smallto-moderate effect sizes (Atari, 2016; Kertechian & Swami, 2017; Swami & Ng, 2015; Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015), suggesting the need to explore sex differences in body appreciation across various national and ethnic groups, considering other variables such as socio-economic status. The research provided evidence of adequate internal consistency, both for the entire sample and for male and female subsamples. Evaluation of correlation coefficients between BAS-2 scores and scores on other measures supported convergent validity of the scale. Higher body appreciation was related to positive body and appearance self-conscious emotions (hubristic and authentic pride), as well as variables referring to well-being (positive affect, self-esteem, and positive orientation), which is in line with previous studies (Alleva et al., 2016; Atari, 2016; Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015). As suggested in previous research, individuals who appreciate their bodies present positive bodyrelated emotions (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015). On the other hand, lower body appreciation was associated with body-related shame and guilt. The results corroborate previously reported relationships of body appreciation with body dissatisfaction, negative body-related emotions, and other negative characteristics (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015). The present study, similarly to other reports (Avalos et al., 2005; Swami et al., 2011), also found negative correlations between body appreciation and BMI. Despite the contribution this study makes to the assessment of positive body image, it has its limitations. First, accidental but not random sampling was used, which may have led to an under/overrepresentation of certain groups within participants. Second, BMI might have been biased by inaccuracies in self-reported weight and height. Third, we did not examine test-retest reliability, which is a more conservative method to estimate reliability than internal consistency coefficients. Fourth, other types of validity were not assessed in the study, whereas evaluation of divergent validity would result in a more comprehensive psychometric description of the Polish BAS-2. Although the findings are consistent with previous research, corroborating the good psychometric properties of the BAS-2, we discern two issues that are worthy of further exploration. First, evidence for a one-factor structure of the BAS-2 in various countries suggests that cross-cultural comparisons of body appreciation can be possible. However, more restrictive levels of measurement invariance should be tested. Second, future studies on scale validity are essential using behavioural indicators (e.g., engagement in physical activity or healthy food consumption). Nonetheless, it may be concluded that the Polish BAS-2 is a psychometrically appropriate measure of body appreciation in Polish-speaking population.
